results.name: first_exposure_minus_repeat_yes_rate
results.description: Per participant (trial_index restart), yes rate on the first trial on which each set appears minus the yes rate on that set's later trials; the model ignores exposure history, so t_observed far from null_mean means first encounters of a set are judged more (above) or less (below) generously than later ones.
results.code:
# name: first_exposure_minus_repeat_yes_rate
# description: Per participant (trial_index restart), yes rate on the first trial on which each set appears minus the yes rate on that set's later trials; the model ignores exposure history, so t_observed far from null_mean means first encounters of a set are judged more (above) or less (below) generously than later ones.
def test_statistic(df):
    ti = df["trial_index"].to_numpy()
    pid = np.cumsum(np.r_[1, (np.diff(ti) < 0).astype(int)])
    tmp = pd.DataFrame({"pid": pid, "s": df["number_set"].astype(str).to_numpy(), "ti": ti, "r": df["rating"].to_numpy(dtype=float)})
    tmp = tmp.sort_values(["pid", "ti"], kind="mergesort")
    first = tmp.groupby(["pid", "s"]).cumcount().to_numpy() == 0
    r = tmp["r"].to_numpy()
    if first.sum() == 0 or (~first).sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[first].mean() - r[~first].mean())

results.name: cell_unanimity_fraction
results.description: Fraction of (set, target) cells answered by >1 response in which all responses agree (all yes or all no); t_observed above null_mean means people are more consistent per item (sharper, less graded endorsement) than the model's probabilities imply, below means less consistent.

results.name: mult4_set_mult4_vs_even_gap
results.description: Among sets of >=2 examples that are all multiples of 4, yes rate for non-example multiple-of-4 targets minus yes rate for even non-multiple-of-4 targets; t_observed below null_mean means people generalize to the broader 'even' concept more (less specific) than the model's size principle predicts, above means more specific.
results.code:
# name: mult4_set_mult4_vs_even_gap
# description: Among sets of >=2 examples that are all multiples of 4, yes rate for non-example multiple-of-4 targets minus yes rate for even non-multiple-of-4 targets; t_observed below null_mean means people generalize to the broader 'even' concept more (less specific) than the model's size principle predicts, above means more specific.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(ex), axis=1)
    m4 = np.all(np.isnan(ex) | (ex % 4 == 0), axis=1) & (n >= 2)
    isex = np.any(ex == t[:, None], axis=1)
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
    a = m4 & ~isex & (t % 4 == 0)
    b = m4 & ~isex & (t % 2 == 0) & (t % 4 != 0)
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: parity_violating_near_yes_rate
results.description: Yes rate for non-example targets of the OPPOSITE parity to all examples, lying within 3 of some example, among sets of >=2 examples that are all even or all odd; t_observed above null_mean means people generalize by numerical proximity despite a parity violation more than the model (whose parity rule swamps intervals) predicts, below means less.
results.code:
# name: parity_violating_near_yes_rate
# description: Yes rate for non-example targets of the OPPOSITE parity to all examples, lying within 3 of some example, among sets of >=2 examples that are all even or all odd; t_observed above null_mean means people generalize by numerical proximity despite a parity violation more than the model (whose parity rule swamps intervals) predicts, below means less.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(ex), axis=1)
    par = np.where(np.isnan(ex), np.nan, ex % 2)
    allsame = (np.nanmin(par, axis=1) == np.nanmax(par, axis=1)) & (n >= 2)
    setpar = np.nanmax(par, axis=1)
    d = np.nanmin(np.abs(ex - t[:, None]), axis=1)
    m = allsame & ((t % 2) != setpar) & (d > 0) & (d <= 3)
    if m.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(df["rating"].to_numpy()[m].mean())

results.name: participant_yes_rate_sd
results.description: SD across participants (identified by trial_index restarting at 0 in row order) of each participant's overall yes rate; the model has no individual differences, so t_observed above null_mean means people differ in generalization breadth more than the model allows.
results.code:
# name: participant_yes_rate_sd
# description: SD across participants (identified by trial_index restarting at 0 in row order) of each participant's overall yes rate; the model has no individual differences, so t_observed above null_mean means people differ in generalization breadth more than the model allows.
def test_statistic(df):
    ti = df["trial_index"].to_numpy()
    pid = np.cumsum(np.r_[1, (np.diff(ti) < 0).astype(int)])
    r = pd.Series(df["rating"].to_numpy(dtype=float)).groupby(pid).mean()
    return float(r.std(ddof=0)) if len(r) > 1 else 0.0

results.name: mixed_parity_interior_gap_yes_rate
results.description: Yes rate for targets strictly inside the range of the examples but more than 8 from every example, among sets of >=3 examples with mixed parity (no parity rule); t_observed below null_mean means people fill gaps between examples less than the model's interval hypotheses predict (similarity-based rather than range-based), above means more.
results.code:
# name: mixed_parity_interior_gap_yes_rate
# description: Yes rate for targets strictly inside the range of the examples but more than 8 from every example, among sets of >=3 examples with mixed parity (no parity rule); t_observed below null_mean means people fill gaps between examples less than the model's interval hypotheses predict (similarity-based rather than range-based), above means more.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(ex), axis=1)
    par = np.where(np.isnan(ex), np.nan, ex % 2)
    mixed = np.nanmin(par, axis=1) != np.nanmax(par, axis=1)
    d = np.nanmin(np.abs(ex - t[:, None]), axis=1)
    inside = (t > np.nanmin(ex, axis=1)) & (t < np.nanmax(ex, axis=1))
    m = mixed & (n >= 3) & inside & (d > 8)
    if m.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(df["rating"].to_numpy()[m].mean())

results.name: last_vs_first_parity_match_gap
results.description: Among sets whose first- and last-shown examples differ in parity, yes rate for non-example targets matching the LAST example's parity minus targets matching the FIRST example's parity; t_observed above null_mean means recency acts on rule (parity) evidence more strongly than the model's fitted order gradient produces, below means less (or primacy).
results.code:
# name: last_vs_first_parity_match_gap
# description: Among sets whose first- and last-shown examples differ in parity, yes rate for non-example targets matching the LAST example's parity minus targets matching the FIRST example's parity; t_observed above null_mean means recency acts on rule (parity) evidence more strongly than the model's fitted order gradient produces, below means less (or primacy).
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(ex), axis=1)
    first = ex[:, 0]
    last = ex[np.arange(len(ex)), n - 1]
    isex = np.any(ex == t[:, None], axis=1)
    m = (n >= 2) & ((first % 2) != (last % 2)) & ~isex
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
    a = m & ((t % 2) == (last % 2))
    b = m & ((t % 2) == (first % 2))
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: cross_set_carryover_effect
results.description: Within participant, yes rate when the immediately preceding trial was a yes on a DIFFERENT set minus when it was a no on a different set; the model treats trials independently (null near its stimulus-driven baseline), so t_observed above null_mean means response perseveration/carryover across sets.
results.code:
# name: cross_set_carryover_effect
# description: Within participant, yes rate when the immediately preceding trial was a yes on a DIFFERENT set minus when it was a no on a different set; the model treats trials independently (null near its stimulus-driven baseline), so t_observed above null_mean means response perseveration/carryover across sets.
def test_statistic(df):
    ti = df["trial_index"].to_numpy()
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
    ok = np.r_[False, (np.diff(ti) == 1) & (s[1:] != s[:-1])]
    prev = np.r_[np.nan, r[:-1]]
    a = ok & (prev == 1)
    b = ok & (prev == 0)
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())
